explain.say: Compare them with insect flowers. Wind flowers need no bright petals, scent or nectar, but they must make huge amounts of pollen, which is why grass pollen fills the air in early summer.

faq.q: Why do wind-pollinated plants make so much pollen?
faq.a: The wind blows pollen everywhere, not just to the right flower, so almost all of it is wasted. Making vast amounts makes it likely that some grains land on a stigma of the same kind of plant.
asks: Why is there so much pollen in the air?

faq.a: A feathery stigma works like a net with a big surface. It hangs out in the moving air and catches passing pollen grains.
asks: What does a feathery stigma do?

faq.a: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen in the air, very often from wind-pollinated grasses and trees. Insect-pollinated flowers rarely cause it, because their pollen is heavier and stickier and does not float far.
asks: Why does pollen make me sneeze?

faq.q: Why do wind-pollinated flowers look dull?
faq.a: They do not need to attract animals, so there is no point spending energy on big coloured petals, scent or nectar. Petals could even block the wind from the anthers.
asks: Why are grass flowers not colourful?

faq.q: What happens after pollen lands on a stigma?
faq.a: The pollen grain grows a thin tube down through the style into the ovary. A male cell travels down it and joins the egg cell in an ovule, which then grows into a seed.

facts: Wind-pollinated plants include grasses, cereals such as wheat and maize, and trees such as oak, birch, hazel and pine.
A single maize plant can release millions of pollen grains.
Grass pollen is one of the most common causes of hay fever.
